sanctuary.explainer: A "sanctuary law" limits how much state and local police can help federal immigration agents. California's main one is [SB 54](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201720180SB54), the California Values Act, passed in 2017.
sanctuary.current_policy: California's baseline is the California Values Act, [SB 54](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201720180SB54) (2017), in effect since January 1, 2018. It says state and local agencies can't use their staff or money to do federal civil immigration enforcement. That means they generally can't hold someone in jail just because ICE asks (called a "detainer" or hold request), can't arrest people on civil immigration warrants, and can't sign "287(g)" agreements — deals that let local officers act as immigration agents. There are exceptions: jails can tell ICE when someone is being released, or hand them over, if that person was convicted of certain serious or violent felonies listed in state law. A separate law, the TRUTH Act ([AB 2792](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201520160AB2792), 2016), says people in custody must be told about, and agree to, any ICE interview, and that local governments must hold a public meeting if they give ICE access. State prisons (CDCR) are only partly covered by SB 54 and follow their own notification rules.
key_facts: [SB 54](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201720180SB54) took effect January 1, 2018. The first Trump administration sued to block it and lost: the case was dismissed, the Ninth Circuit appeals court agreed, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear it — so the law still stands.

287(g) agreements (which deputize local officers to do immigration enforcement) are banned for California agencies under SB 54. In 2025, an attempt by Shasta County's sheriff was paused because it conflicted with state law.
SB 54's exceptions let agencies notify or hand someone to ICE if that person was convicted of specific serious or violent felonies — not for people whose only issue is their immigration status.
The TRUTH Act (2016) requires that people be told they can decline an ICE jail interview, and requires a public community meeting when local agencies give ICE access.

Sanctuary rules are mostly set by state law, so a governor's main tools are enforcement guidance, the attorney general's approach to lawsuits, prison rules, and signing or vetoing new bills — not repealing the law directly.
sanctuary.comparison: California is among the states that most limit local cooperation with immigration agents, alongside Illinois (the TRUST Act) and several others. By contrast, states like Texas (with its SB 4 law) and Florida require local agencies to cooperate with ICE and ban sanctuary policies. The federal 287(g) program had agreements with roughly 1,600 agencies nationwide by 2026 — almost none in California.
sanctuary.arguments_for_change: People who want stronger sanctuary protections argue that keeping local police out of immigration enforcement builds trust, so immigrant crime victims and witnesses will feel safe reporting crimes. They note that ICE detainers usually aren't signed by a judge, which raises constitutional concerns and can expose counties to lawsuits. And they point out that the existing felony exceptions already allow cooperation in the most serious cases — so further steps (like limiting data sharing, or keeping ICE out of courthouses, schools, and hospitals) would only affect civil enforcement.
sanctuary.arguments_against_change: People who want fuller cooperation with ICE argue that releasing people ICE has flagged — including some with past criminal records that don't fit the exceptions — can send people federal authorities believe are deportable back into communities. They say planned handoffs from jail are safer for officers and the public than ICE making arrests out on the street, and that immigration enforcement is a federal job the state shouldn't get in the way of. In their view, turning down ICE requests hurts public safety and federal-state teamwork.

gun_policy.current_policy: California has some of the strictest gun laws in the country. The Roberti-Roos Assault Weapons Control Act (1989) and later laws ban many semiautomatic "assault weapons," and the state caps magazines at 10 rounds. In 2022, the U.S. Supreme Court case NYSRPA v. Bruen struck down rules that let officials decide who had a "good enough reason" to carry a concealed gun. In response, [SB 2](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB2) (2023, effective January 1, 2024) switched California to "shall-issue" permits — meaning anyone who qualifies gets one — while adding a 16-hour training requirement and a long list of "sensitive places" where guns are banned even with a permit. A separate law, [AB 28](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB28) (2023, effective 2024), added an 11% state tax on gun and ammunition sales to fund violence-prevention and school-safety programs.
key_facts: California has banned "assault weapons" since the 1989 Roberti-Roos Act and limits magazines to 10 rounds.

[SB 2](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB2) (effective January 1, 2024) kept shall-issue permits after the Bruen ruling but named about 26 categories of "sensitive places." In 2025 the Ninth Circuit appeals court upheld some of those location bans and blocked others while the case continues.

[AB 28](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB28)'s 11% tax on guns and ammunition (effective 2024) is projected to raise about $160 million a year for violence-prevention and school-safety programs. It faces an unresolved court challenge.

Microstamping and other manufacturer-side rules (such as [SB 452](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB452), 2023) are still on the books, though some parts only kick in if the technology is found workable.

Several California gun laws are in active litigation in the Ninth Circuit under the Bruen test — which asks whether a law fits the nation's "history and tradition" of gun regulation — so which rules can actually be enforced shifts as courts rule.
gun_policy.comparison: Independent and advocacy scorecards consistently rank California's gun laws the strictest, or nearly the strictest, in the country — alongside Massachusetts, New York, Illinois, and Connecticut. By contrast, "constitutional carry" states like Texas, Arizona, and Idaho require no permit to carry a concealed gun and have far fewer limits on magazines and rifle types.
gun_policy.arguments_for_change: People who want more restrictions point out that states with stronger gun laws tend to report lower gun-death rates. They argue that the assault-weapon and magazine limits, SB 2's sensitive-places list, and the AB 28 tax cut down gun availability in risky settings while paying for prevention. They say closing remaining gaps — and defending current laws in court — saves lives, and that the Second Amendment still allows reasonable regulation.
gun_policy.arguments_against_change: People who oppose more restrictions argue that California already has the nation's strictest rules yet still has gun crime, so the payoff from new limits is small. They say the post-Bruen court rulings suggest several of California's laws may be unconstitutional and invite expensive lawsuits. They argue that broad sensitive-place bans and a sales tax burden law-abiding gun owners and make carry rights depend on where you are. And they say enforcement is better aimed at illegal trafficking and people already barred from owning guns than at lawful buyers.

policing.current_policy: California has passed a series of police-accountability laws while leaving most funding and prosecution decisions to local agencies and elected district attorneys. [AB 392](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB392) (2019) raised the bar for when police can use deadly force — to when it's "necessary" to stop an immediate threat, instead of the older, looser "reasonable" standard. [SB 2](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB2) (2021), the Kenneth Ross Jr. Police Decertification Act, set up a statewide process to strip ("decertify") officers of their license for serious misconduct and report those who leave to a national database. [AB 1506](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1506) (2020) requires the state Department of Justice to investigate police shootings that kill unarmed civilians. The state prison population has dropped sharply since the 2011 "Realignment" ([AB 109](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201120120AB109)) shifted lower-level felons from state prisons to counties.
key_facts: [AB 392](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB392) (2019) set a "necessary" standard for police deadly force — one of the stricter use-of-force laws in the country.

[SB 2](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB2) (2021) gave the state's police-standards board (POST) the power to decertify officers for serious misconduct. Decertified officers can't be rehired and are listed on the National Decertification Index.

[AB 1506](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1506) (2020) requires the state Department of Justice to investigate fatal police shootings of unarmed civilians.

California's prison population fell to about 90,600 by December 2025 — roughly 27% below December 2019 — after the 2011 Realignment ([AB 109](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201120120AB109)) and pandemic-era reductions. The state has closed multiple prisons.

California's imprisonment rate was about 294 per 100,000 adults in 2025, down from a peak of over 173,000 total prisoners in 2006. Police staffing and budgets are set locally, so a governor's direct control is limited.
policing.comparison: California's "necessary" use-of-force standard and statewide decertification system are stronger than those in many states, though states like Colorado and New Jersey adopted similar reforms after 2020. California's imprisonment rate sits near or a bit below the national average — and well below high-incarceration states like Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas.
policing.arguments_for_change: People who favor reducing incarceration and using alternatives argue that California's prison population dropped a lot after Realignment without a lasting rise in violent crime — suggesting many people can be safely supervised in their communities. They say diversion programs, mental-health and addiction treatment, and reentry help address root causes more cheaply than prison, and that strong accountability rules (AB 392, SB 2) build community trust and cut down on costly misconduct.
policing.arguments_against_change: People who favor more funding and stricter penalties argue that having enough officers and clear consequences deters crime and reassures victims. They note that some types of crime rose during the reform years and say visible enforcement is needed for public confidence. They warn that accountability mandates and lower incarceration, if not matched with enough police and supervision resources, can strain departments and let repeat offenders cycle through. In their view, public safety shouldn't be traded away to lower prison numbers.

prop36_47.explainer: [Prop 47](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2014/prop-47-110414.aspx) (2014) turned several lower-level drug and theft crimes from felonies into misdemeanors and set the felony shoplifting line at $950. [Prop 36](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2024/Prop36-110524.pdf) (2024) partly reversed that — it lets prosecutors file felony charges against repeat theft offenders and toughens some drug penalties.
prop36_47.current_policy: [Prop 47](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2014/prop-47-110414.aspx) (November 2014) reclassified several nonviolent drug-possession and theft crimes from felonies to misdemeanors — including setting the felony shoplifting/theft line at $950 — and put the savings toward treatment and victim programs. [Prop 36](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2024/Prop36-110524.pdf) (November 2024), which passed about 70% to 30% and took effect December 18, 2024, partly rolled that back. It allows felony charges for petty theft when someone has two or more prior theft convictions, lets prosecutors add up the value of multiple thefts to cross the $950 line, raises penalties for certain fentanyl and other drug crimes, and creates a "treatment-mandated felony" that gives repeat drug offenders a choice between treatment and incarceration.
key_facts: [Prop 47](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2014/prop-47-110414.aspx) (2014) set the felony theft line at $950 and dropped certain drug-possession and theft felonies to misdemeanors.
[Prop 36](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2024/Prop36-110524.pdf) (2024) passed about 70% to 30% and took effect December 18, 2024.
Prop 36 allows felony charges for theft under $950 when the person has two or more prior theft convictions, and lets values from multiple incidents be added together.

Per PPIC, California's 2024 property-crime rate fell about 9.9% to roughly 2,084 per 100,000 — its lowest since 1985 — while reported shoplifting rose about 14.2% (combined retail theft up about 3%). These trends came before Prop 36 took effect.

PPIC research credits the post-2019 rise in retail theft more to pandemic-era criminal-justice responses than to Prop 47 itself, and finds that a higher chance of getting caught deters crime more than longer sentences do.
prop36_47.comparison: After Prop 47, California's $950 felony-theft line was in the middle of the national range — higher than states like New Jersey ($200) but lower than the misdemeanor ceiling in Texas, which uses graduated tiers (felonies start around $2,500). Prop 36 didn't lower the dollar figure; instead it narrowed the misdemeanor rule for repeat offenders. Many states revisited their theft and drug-sentencing thresholds in the 2020s.
prop36_47.arguments_for_change: People who want to keep or expand Prop 47 argue that property crime hit multi-decade lows in 2024 even before Prop 36 took effect, that lower incarceration freed up money for treatment and victim services, and that PPIC and other research find certainty of getting caught deters crime more than longer sentences. So, they argue, more decriminalization and diversion could lower incarceration without raising crime.
prop36_47.arguments_against_change: People who want to roll back further argue that reported shoplifting and some retail thefts kept climbing after 2019, and that the $950 misdemeanor line let repeat offenders dodge real consequences. They say Prop 36's nearly 70% approval shows broad public worry about open drug use and theft, and that felony exposure for repeat offenders — plus treatment-mandated felonies — gives leverage to push chronic offenders into treatment and to deter organized retail theft.
